title: Ratio & Proportion
description: Simplifying ratios, dividing quantities, direct and inverse proportion, and real-world applications.

notes.heading: Simplifying Ratios
notes.body:
A ratio compares two or more quantities. It shows the relative size of each part, not the actual amounts.

📌 Definition
A ratio of $a$ to $b$ is written $a:b$ or as the fraction $\dfrac{a}{b}$. It is in simplest form when the highest common factor (HCF) of all terms is $1$.

🔑 How it works
To simplify a ratio:
1. Make sure all quantities are in the same units.
2. Divide every term by their HCF.
3. Write the final ratio using whole numbers only.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Simplifying a two-part ratio
Simplify $56:84$.

The HCF of $56$ and $84$ is $28$.
$$56:84 = \dfrac{56}{28}:\dfrac{84}{28} = 2:3$$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Same units first
Simplify $750\text{ g}:1.5\text{ kg}$.

First convert to grams: $1.5\text{ kg} = 1500\text{ g}$.
The ratio becomes $750:1500$. The HCF is $750$.
$$750:1500 = 1:2$$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Trying to simplify before converting units. $750\text{ g}:1.5\text{ kg}$ is NOT $750:1.5$; the units must match first.

✅ Tip
If the HCF is not obvious, simplify in stages: divide by $2$, then by $3$, etc., until no common factor remains.

notes.heading: Dividing a Quantity in a Given Ratio
notes.body:
When a total amount is shared in a given ratio, each part receives a fraction of the whole equal to its share of the total parts.

📌 Definition
If a quantity $Q$ is divided in the ratio $a:b$, then:
$$\text{first share} = \dfrac{a}{a+b} \times Q, \quad \text{second share} = \dfrac{b}{a+b} \times Q$$
For three parts $a:b:c$, the denominator is $a+b+c$.

🔑 Step-by-Step Method
1. Add the parts of the ratio to find the total number of shares.
2. Divide the quantity by the total shares to find the value of one share.
3. Multiply each part of the ratio by the value of one share.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Sharing money
Divide £$450$ in the ratio $4:5$.

Total shares $= 4 + 5 = 9$.
Value of one share $= 450 \div 9 = 50$.
First share $= 4 \times 50 = 200$.
Second share $= 5 \times 50 = 250$.
So the amounts are £$200$ and £$250$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Given one share, find the total
The ratio of red to blue sweets is $3:7$. If there are $42$ blue sweets, how many sweets are there altogether?

Blue sweets represent $7$ shares, so $7$ shares $= 42$.
One share $= 42 \div 7 = 6$.
Total shares $= 3 + 7 = 10$.
Total sweets $= 10 \times 6 = 60$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The order of the ratio matters: $4:5$ is not the same as $5:4$.
• Always check that the shares add up to the original total.
• If a ratio is not in simplest form, simplify it first or work with the given numbers — both methods give the same final shares.

notes.heading: Equivalent Ratios and the Unitary Method
notes.body:
Equivalent ratios describe the same relationship using different numbers. The unitary method uses this idea by first finding the value of one unit.

📌 Definition
Two ratios are equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by multiplying or dividing every term by the same non-zero number.
$$a:b = ka:kb \quad \text{for any } k \neq 0$$

🔑 The Unitary Method
1. Find the value of one unit by division.
2. Multiply by the number of units you need.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Cost scaling
If $7$ notebooks cost £$22.40$, how much do $11$ notebooks cost?

Cost of one notebook $= 22.40 \div 7 = 3.20$.
Cost of $11$ notebooks $= 11 \times 3.20 = 35.20$.
So $11$ notebooks cost £$35.20$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Ratio from a total
A fruit drink is made by mixing orange juice and water in the ratio $2:5$. How much orange juice is needed for $3.5$ litres of drink?

Total parts $= 2 + 5 = 7$.
One part $= 3.5 \div 7 = 0.5$ litres.
Orange juice $= 2 \times 0.5 = 1$ litre.

✅ Check
$1$ litre of orange juice and $2.5$ litres of water give $3.5$ litres in total, and $1:2.5 = 2:5$ after multiplying by $2$. ✓

⚠️ Common Misconception
Thinking that $2:5$ means orange juice is $\dfrac{2}{5}$ of the drink. It is actually $\dfrac{2}{7}$ of the drink because the total parts are $7$.

notes.heading: Direct Proportion
notes.body:
Two quantities are in direct proportion when they increase or decrease at the same rate. Their graph is a straight line through the origin.

📌 Definition
$y$ is directly proportional to $x$ if:
$$y = kx \quad \text{or} \quad \dfrac{y}{x} = k$$
where $k$ is the constant of proportionality.

🔑 How it works
• If $x$ doubles, $y$ doubles.
• If $x$ triples, $y$ triples.
• The ratio $\dfrac{y}{x}$ is always the same.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Finding the constant
$y$ is directly proportional to $x$. When $x = 6$, $y = 15$. Find $y$ when $x = 14$.

Step 1: Find $k$.
$$k = \dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{15}{6} = 2.5$$

Step 2: Write the equation.
$$y = 2.5x$$

Step 3: Substitute $x = 14$.
$$y = 2.5 \times 14 = 35$$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Real-world direct proportion
A car travels $240$ km on $20$ litres of fuel. How far will it travel on $35$ litres at the same rate?

Distance per litre $= 240 \div 20 = 12$ km/litre.
Distance on $35$ litres $= 12 \times 35 = 420$ km.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Direct proportion always passes through $(0,0)$.
• Use $k$ to write a formula and then substitute.
• The symbol $\propto$ means "is proportional to": $y \propto x$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using addition instead of multiplication. If $x$ increases by a factor, multiply $y$ by the same factor; do not add the same amount.

notes.heading: Inverse Proportion
notes.body:
Two quantities are in inverse proportion when one increases as the other decreases. Their product is constant.

📌 Definition
$y$ is inversely proportional to $x$ if:
$$y = \dfrac{k}{x} \quad \text{or} \quad xy = k$$
where $k$ is the constant of proportionality.

🔑 How it works
• If $x$ doubles, $y$ halves.
• If $x$ triples, $y$ becomes one third.
• The product $xy$ never changes.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Finding the constant
$y$ is inversely proportional to $x$. When $x = 8$, $y = 6$. Find $y$ when $x = 12$.

Step 1: Find $k$.
$$k = xy = 8 \times 6 = 48$$

Step 2: Write the equation.
$$y = \dfrac{48}{x}$$

Step 3: Substitute $x = 12$.
$$y = \dfrac{48}{12} = 4$$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Workers and time
$5$ workers take $12$ days to build a wall. How long would $8$ workers take at the same rate?

Total work $= 5 \times 12 = 60$ worker-days.
Time for $8$ workers $= 60 \div 8 = 7.5$ days.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Inverse proportion gives a curved graph that never touches either axis.
• Always check whether the product $xy$ stays constant.
• Inverse proportion appears in speed–time problems for a fixed distance: $s \times t = d$.

⚠️ Common Misconception
Treating inverse proportion like direct proportion. If the number of workers increases, the time decreases, so dividing is correct, not multiplying.

notes.heading: Map Scales and Scale Factors
notes.body:
A scale compares a measurement on a map, plan, or model to the corresponding real measurement. Scales are usually written as ratios.

📌 Definition
A scale of $1:n$ means $1$ unit on the map represents $n$ units in reality.
$$\text{real distance} = \text{map distance} \times n$$

🔑 Length, Area, and Volume Scale Factors
For a scale ratio $1:n$:
• Length scale factor $= n$
• Area scale factor $= n^2$
• Volume scale factor $= n^3$

💡 Worked Example 1 — Map distance to real distance
A map has scale $1:25\,000$. Two towns are $8$ cm apart on the map. What is the real distance in km?

Real distance $= 8 \times 25\,000 = 200\,000$ cm.
Convert to km: $200\,000$ cm $= 2$ km.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Scale model area
A model car is built to a scale of $1:18$. The area of the model's windscreen is $12$ cm$^2$. What is the real windscreen area?

Area scale factor $= 18^2 = 324$.
Real area $= 12 \times 324 = 3\,888$ cm$^2$.

✅ Check
$3\,888$ cm$^2 = 0.3888$ m$^2$, which is sensible for a car windscreen.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using the length scale factor for area or volume. Area scales by $n^2$ and volume by $n^3$, so never forget to square or cube the scale factor.

notes.heading: Best Value, Exchange Rates, and Mixed Ratio Problems
notes.body:
Ratios and proportions appear everywhere in everyday decisions, from choosing the cheapest pack size to converting currencies.

📌 Definition
Best value means getting the most product for the least money. Compare unit prices:
$$\text{unit price} = \dfrac{\text{total cost}}{\text{number of units or mass}}$$

🔑 Exchange Rates
An exchange rate is a ratio between two currencies. To convert:
$$\text{amount in new currency} = \text{amount in original currency} \times \text{exchange rate}$$

💡 Worked Example 1 — Best buy
A $400$ g bag of rice costs £$1.60$ and a $750$ g bag costs £$2.70$. Which is better value?

Small bag unit price: £$1.60 \div 400 = 0.0040$ per gram.
Large bag unit price: £$2.70 \div 750 = 0.0036$ per gram.
The $750$ g bag is better value because each gram costs less.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Currency conversion
The exchange rate is £1 = ＄1.25. Convert £$80$ to dollars.

$$80 \times 1.25 = 100$$
So £80 = ＄100.

💡 Worked Example 3 — Recipe scaling
A recipe for $6$ people uses $300$ g of flour. How much flour is needed for $10$ people?

Flour per person $= 300 \div 6 = 50$ g.
For $10$ people: $10 \times 50 = 500$ g.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always use the same units when comparing ratios or unit prices.
• Write the exchange rate as a ratio, e.g. $1:1.25$, and multiply or divide consistently.
• Scaling recipes, maps, and models all use the same proportional reasoning.

✅ Tip
A quick sanity check: the larger pack is not always cheaper per unit. Always calculate the unit price before deciding.

A ratio whose terms have no common factor other than $1$.
Ratios that represent the same relationship after multiplying or dividing every term by the same non-zero number.
Splitting a total quantity into shares according to the parts of the ratio.
Finding the value of one unit first, then scaling to any number of units.
flashcards.example: $5$ tickets cost £$60$, so $1$ ticket costs £$12$ and $8$ tickets cost £$96$.

The fixed value $k$ that links two proportional quantities.
One quantity increases as the other decreases; their product is constant, $xy = k$ or $y = \dfrac{k}{x}$.
A ratio comparing a distance on a map to the corresponding real-world distance.
flashcards.example: $1:50\,000$ means $2$ cm on the map represents $1$ km in reality.

flashcards.definition: For a scale $1:n$, area scales by $n^2$.
flashcards.example: A model scale of $1:10$ gives an area scale factor of $100$.

flashcards.definition: The option with the lowest cost per unit of measurement.
flashcards.example: $500$ g for £$2$ is £$0.004$/g; $750$ g for £$2.70$ is £$0.0036$/g, so the $750$ g pack is better value.

flashcards.definition: A ratio that converts an amount from one currency to another.

questions.explanation: The HCF of $72$ and $90$ is $18$. Dividing both terms by $18$ gives $4:5$.
There are $3 + 4 = 7$ shares, so one share is £$168 \div 7 = 24$. The shares are £$3 \times 24 = 72$ and £$4 \times 24 = 96$.

questions.stem: If $9$ books cost £$54$, how much do $13$ books cost?
questions.explanation: One book costs £$54 \div 9 = 6$. Therefore $13$ books cost £$13 \times 6 = 78$.

questions.stem: A recipe for $4$ people needs $600$ g of pasta. How much pasta is needed for $9$ people?
questions.explanation: Pasta per person is $600 \div 4 = 150$ g. For $9$ people, $9 \times 150 = 1350$ g.

questions.stem: $y$ is directly proportional to $x$. When $x = 8$, $y = 28$. Find $y$ when $x = 14$.
$y$ is inversely proportional to $x$. When $x = 5$, $y = 16$. Find $y$ when $x = 10$.
A map has scale $1:40\,000$. A road is $6$ cm long on the map. What is the real distance in km?
questions.explanation: Real distance $= 6 \times 40\,000 = 240\,000$ cm. Converting to km gives $240\,000 \div 100\,000 = 2.4$ km.

questions.stem: A model boat is built to a scale of $1:25$. The real deck area is $1250$ m$^2$. What is the model deck area in m$^2$?
questions.explanation: Area scale factor is $25^2 = 625$. Model area $= 1250 \div 625 = 2$ m$^2$.

questions.stem: Which is better value: $300$ g for £$1.80$ or $500$ g for £$2.70$?
choices: 300 g because the total cost is lower
500 g because the price per gram is lower
You cannot tell without more information
questions.explanation: Unit prices are £$1.80 \div 300 = 0.006$/g and £$2.70 \div 500 = 0.0054$/g. The $500$ g pack is cheaper per gram.

questions.stem: The ratio of boys to girls in a club is $5:6$. If there are $45$ boys, how many girls are there?
questions.explanation: $5$ shares represent $45$ boys, so one share is $45 \div 5 = 9$. Girls are $6 \times 9 = 54$.

questions.stem: The exchange rate is £1 = ＄1.28. Convert £$120$ to dollars.
Two numbers are in the ratio $7:3$ and their difference is $36$. Find the larger number.
questions.explanation: The difference between the parts is $7 - 3 = 4$ shares, so $4$ shares $= 36$ and one share $= 9$. The larger number is $7 \times 9 = 63$.

questions.stem: A car uses $18$ litres of petrol for $270$ km. How many litres are needed for $450$ km at the same rate?
questions.explanation: Litres per km $= 18 \div 270 = \dfrac{1}{15}$. For $450$ km, $450 \times \dfrac{1}{15} = 30$ litres.

questions.stem: A factory order is completed by $6$ machines in $8$ hours. How long would $4$ machines take, assuming inverse proportion?
questions.explanation: Total machine-hours $= 6 \times 8 = 48$. With $4$ machines, time $= 48 \div 4 = 12$ hours.

questions.stem: A paint mixture uses blue and yellow in the ratio $2:5$. A second batch uses $3$ times as much blue as the first batch. If the first batch contained $700$ ml of yellow, how much yellow is needed for the second batch?
questions.explanation: First batch: $5$ shares $= 700$ ml, so one share is $140$ ml and blue is $2 \times 140 = 280$ ml. Second batch blue $= 3 \times 280 = 840$ ml. Since blue is $2$ shares, one share is $420$ ml, so yellow is $5 \times 420 = 2100$ ml.
